beginner: Apricot wants a deep soil that drains fast and lets air reach the roots. Good drainage is the one rule you cannot bend with apricot, because it has little tolerance for wet, heavy ground and the root and crown rots that follow it. A sandy loam is a great fit, and a lighter sandy soil works if you keep up with water. Heavy clay that holds water is the trouble spot; on clay, plant on a raised mound so the roots sit above the soggy soil, and choose a plum rootstock (Myrobalan or Marianna) that takes heavier ground. One apricot quirk: in the alkaline soils of the arid West it is prone to iron chlorosis, where the leaves yellow between green veins, so a near-neutral soil with some compost suits it best.
seasoned: Apricot demands a deep, well-drained loam with good aeration; drainage is the non-negotiable, since it has little tolerance for wet or heavy soils and waterlogging brings on crown and root rot. A sandy loam is well suited and a lighter sandy soil is workable with attention to water. Heavy, water-holding clay is the problem texture; on such ground, plant on a raised berm and pair the tree with a heavier-soil-tolerant plum rootstock (Myrobalan or Marianna 2624) rather than a drainage-fussy seedling stock. Note the apricot-specific weakness: on the high-pH soils of the arid West it is prone to iron chlorosis (interveinal yellowing), so a near-neutral, moderately fertile soil is ideal.

beginner: Apricot grows best in a near-neutral soil, around pH 6.0 to 7.0, and tolerates from about 6.0 to 8.0 (pH just measures how acidic or alkaline the soil is). It leans more tolerant of alkaline soil than most stone fruit, but on strongly alkaline western soils it often shows iron chlorosis, a yellowing between the leaf veins. Test your soil before planting and adjust slowly if needed: garden lime raises the pH if the soil is too acidic, and elemental sulfur lowers it if it is too alkaline. Mix any of this in before you plant, because pH changes slowly and is far easier to fix before the permanent tree goes in.
seasoned: Apricot does best in a near-neutral soil, roughly pH 6.0 to 7.0, and tolerates about 6.0 to 8.0. It is somewhat more alkaline-tolerant than peach or cherry, but on the high-pH soils of the arid West it is notably prone to iron chlorosis (interveinal yellowing). Test the soil before planting and adjust gradually if needed: lime raises a too-acidic pH, elemental sulfur lowers one that is too alkaline. Work amendments in ahead of planting, since pH shifts slowly and is far easier to correct before the permanent tree is in the ground.

beginner: Feed once in early spring before the tree starts growing. Scatter the fertilizer evenly on the soil around the tree out to where the branches reach, keep it off the trunk, and water it in. Apricot does not need heavy feeding, so go light: if the tree is making plenty of new growth, it may need none at all. If the leaves yellow between the veins (common on western alkaline soils), that is an iron problem, not a nitrogen one, so use a chelated iron product instead of more fertilizer. Never feed late in the year, because soft late growth gets damaged by winter cold.
seasoned: Feed lightly in early spring before growth begins, broadcasting evenly around the root zone out to the drip line, off the trunk, and watering it in. Apricot needs modest nitrogen: judge by shoot growth and ease off if the tree is already vigorous. On the alkaline soils of the arid West, watch for iron chlorosis (interveinal yellowing) and correct it with a chelated iron rather than piling on nitrogen. Never feed late in the season, since late nitrogen pushes soft growth that winter cold injures and that canker enters.

beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 (the three numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) works for backyard apricots, used sparingly. Do not overdo nitrogen, the first number, because too much pushes leafy growth that is more prone to disease and winter damage.
seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 suits backyard apricots, applied modestly. Avoid high-nitrogen feeding, which drives soft, disease-prone, overly vigorous growth at the expense of fruiting and winter hardiness.

beginner: A simple guide is a small handful of 10-10-10 for each year of the tree's age, up to a modest amount, spread once in early spring before the buds open. Do not put fertilizer in the planting hole or feed right at planting; wait until the tree starts growing. If the tree is already growing more than a foot of new branch each year, it probably needs little or no feeding at all.
seasoned: A common home rate is about 1/2 to 1 pound of actual nitrogen equivalent scaled to tree age, applied once in early spring before bud break, kept modest because apricot fruits on long-lived spurs and does not need the heavy nitrogen a peach does. Do not fertilize at planting or place fertilizer in the hole; wait until growth begins. Judge by shoot growth: a bearing tree wants roughly 12 to 18 inches of new wood a year.

beginner: Apricot is self-fruitful, which means one tree makes fruit on its own and you do not need a second tree to pollinate it. A few varieties, notably Moorpark, set a heavier crop when a second apricot blooms nearby, but even they fruit alone, so a lone tree is fine. Beyond that, what matters for a tree is the root zone, not the usual vegetable pairings: keep grass and weeds pulled back from under the branches, since lawn competes hard with a young tree, and a mulched, weed-free area helps it settle in. The one site rule is replant disease: do not plant an apricot where another apricot, peach, plum, cherry, or nectarine was recently growing.
seasoned: Apricot is self-fruitful, so a single tree sets a crop on its own with no pollinizer required; a handful of cultivars (Moorpark is the classic) set more heavily with a compatible second variety, but none actually need one. Past pollination, the interactions that matter for a tree are at the root zone, not classic vegetable companions: keep turf and weeds cleared back from under the canopy, since they compete hard with a young tree, and a mulched, competition-free root area establishes it faster. The one site rule is replant disease: do not follow stone fruit with stone fruit on the same ground.

beginner: On small developing apricots, look for a curved, crescent-shaped scar, the mark the beetle leaves when it lays an egg. Damaged fruit often drops early, and some that stays on the tree ends up misshapen or has a grub inside. You see this soon after the petals fall.
seasoned: Small young fruit carries a distinctive crescent-shaped scar where the female cut a slit to lay an egg. Infested fruit often drops early; fruit that hangs on may be gnarled or have a grub tunneling inside near the pit. Damage appears shortly after petal fall and is heaviest east of the Rockies.

beginner: A small beetle with a long snout called the plum curculio. The adults show up around bloom and start damaging the little fruits right after the petals drop, laying eggs inside them. The larvae then feed within the fruit. It is mostly an eastern problem and rare in dry western climates.
seasoned: The plum curculio (Conotrachelus nenuphar), a small snout beetle native to eastern North America. Adults emerge around bloom and attack fruit from petal fall onward, laying eggs in the developing fruit; the larvae feed inside. There is little pressure in the arid West.

beginner: Early in the morning the beetles are slow. Spread a sheet under the tree, tap the branches so the beetles fall, and destroy them. Pick up and throw away any dropped fruit promptly so the larvae inside do not mature. A kaolin clay spray (a fine white mineral coating) starting at petal fall helps keep them off.
seasoned: For a backyard tree, jarring the limbs over a sheet in the early morning when the beetles are sluggish, then destroying what drops, reduces the population. Promptly gather and dispose of dropped infested fruit to break the cycle. Kaolin clay applied from petal fall is an organic deterrent.

beginner: The main thing is cleanup. Pick up fallen fruit all season so the larvae inside cannot finish growing in the soil under the tree. Keeping the ground clear lowers the number of beetles the next year.
seasoned: Sanitation is the backbone: remove dropped fruit through the season so larvae cannot complete development in the soil beneath the tree. A clean orchard floor and prompt fruit pickup steadily lower pressure year over year.

beginner: Look at the very bottom of the trunk where it meets the soil. Peachtree borers leave a sticky, gummy ooze mixed with what looks like wet sawdust (called frass). You may see a small mound of gum and frass at the base. A young tree with several borers can be killed in one season, so this is one to catch early.
seasoned: Gummy ooze mixed with sawdust-like frass at the base of the trunk, right around the soil line, often with a mounded look where the bark meets the ground. Larvae tunnel the inner bark at the crown; several borers can girdle and kill a young apricot in a single season, and the wounds also open the door to canker.

beginner: The larvae (young, grub-like stage) of the peachtree borer, a moth whose adults look like wasps and fly during the day. The adults lay eggs on the lower trunk in summer, and the larvae burrow into the bark at and below the soil line. Trees with existing wounds are hit hardest, but a healthy tree can be attacked too.
seasoned: Larvae of the peachtree borer (Synanthedon exitiosa), a clearwing moth whose adults are day-flying and wasp-like. Eggs are laid on the lower trunk in summer; the larvae tunnel the inner bark at and just below the soil line. It attacks all stone fruit, apricot included, and hits stressed or wounded trees first.

beginner: Once the larvae are inside, no spray reaches them. The backyard fix is to scrape soil away from the base in late summer or fall, find the holes marked by gum and frass, and kill the larvae with a thin, stiff wire pushed into each hole. Then smooth the soil back. Avoid nicking the trunk base with mowers or trimmers.
seasoned: There is no rescue spray once larvae are tunneling inside. The practical home control is to expose the crown in late summer or fall, find the entry holes by the gum and frass, and kill larvae by hand with a thin wire (worming). Keep the trunk base free of wounds and paint it white against sunscald cracks.

beginner: Keep mowers and string trimmers away from the trunk; the wounds they leave attract the egg-laying moths, and white trunk paint prevents the sunburn cracks they enter. Keep grass and weeds cleared from the base so you can see the soil line, and check it every late summer for fresh gummy ooze.
seasoned: Protect the lower trunk from mechanical injury and sunscald (a white trunk paint helps), keep the tree vigorous, and clear weeds and tall grass from the base so the crown stays open and easy to inspect. Check the soil line each late summer for fresh gum so an infestation is caught in its first year.

beginner: Clusters of small green or gray soft-bodied insects on the tips of new spring growth, curling and twisting the young leaves, with a sticky coating below that turns black and moldy. It is worst on young trees and mainly stunts new growth rather than ruining fruit.
seasoned: Dense colonies of green or mealy-gray aphids on the tips of new spring shoots, curling and distorting young leaves, with sticky honeydew below that blackens into sooty mold. Heaviest on vigorous young trees; it slows shoot growth but rarely harms fruit directly.

beginner: Small sap-sucking insects (green peach aphid and mealy plum aphid). Their eggs overwinter on the tree and the young hatch to feed on the soft new spring growth. The numbers usually drop on their own by midsummer as the shoots toughen and ladybugs and other helpers move in.
seasoned: Chiefly the green peach aphid and the mealy plum aphid. They overwinter as eggs on the tree and explode on the tender spring flush, feeding on sap; populations usually crash by midsummer as shoots harden and natural enemies build up.

beginner: Often you can leave it alone, since ladybugs and other helpers clear it by midsummer. On a young tree that is badly hit, blast the colonies off with a hose, or spray the curled tips with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil. Do not over-fertilize, since lush new growth is what the aphids love.
seasoned: Often no action is needed, since beneficials clean it up by midsummer. For a heavy infestation on a young tree, a strong jet of water knocks colonies off, or insecticidal soap or horticultural oil applied to the curled tips works; protect the ladybugs and lacewings that do most of the control. Avoid high-nitrogen feeding, which fuels the soft growth aphids prefer.

beginner: Avoid heavy feeding that pushes the soft growth aphids love, welcome ladybugs and lacewings, and do not panic over the spring leaf-curl, which usually does not hurt the crop. A dormant oil spray in late winter cuts down the overwintering eggs.
seasoned: Keep trees vigorous but not over-fed (high nitrogen invites aphids), encourage beneficial insects, and tolerate the early-season curl, which rarely affects the crop. A dormant oil spray reduces overwintering eggs where the pest is chronic.

beginner: Tiny gray bumps crusting the bark of twigs and branches, and small red-ringed spots on the fruit. A bad case can weaken branches and even kill them, and it spots the fruit. The scales are easy to miss because each one is barely the size of a pinhead.
seasoned: Tiny gray, cone-shaped scales encrusting bark on twigs and scaffolds, sometimes with a reddish halo, and small red-ringed spots on the fruit skin. Heavy infestations weaken and can kill branches, and the fruit blemishes downgrade the crop.

beginner: A tiny armored insect called San Jose scale that sits under a waxy cover and sucks sap from the bark. It has several rounds a year. The young, called crawlers, are the only stage that moves around and the only one a spray can hit.
seasoned: San Jose scale (Diaspidiotus perniciosus), an armored scale insect that feeds on sap under a waxy cover. It has several overlapping generations a year; the mobile crawler stage is the point at which it spreads and the only stage a spray reaches.

beginner: The main control is a good horticultural oil spray while the tree is bare and dormant, coating the twigs and branches to smother the scale. During the season, prune out and destroy any branches that are heavily crusted. Keeping the tree open and vigorous helps.
seasoned: A thorough dormant-season horticultural oil spray, applied to the leafless tree so it coats twigs and scaffolds, smothers overwintering scale and is the mainstay backyard control. In-season, time any additional oil to the crawler stage. Prune out and destroy heavily encrusted wood.

beginner: A yearly dormant oil spray in late winter keeps scale from building up. Avoid harsh insecticides so the natural enemies that eat scale can do their work, and keep the tree pruned open so any spray reaches all the bark.
seasoned: An annual dormant oil spray keeps scale from building up. Encourage the tiny parasitic wasps and predatory beetles that attack scale by avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides, and prune to keep the canopy open and easy to cover thoroughly.

beginner: Ripe apricots have sunken, puckered, dimpled patches, a look growers call catfacing. It comes from insects feeding on the fruit when it was small. The fruit is still usable; the damage is mostly on the surface and does not spread.
seasoned: Mature fruit shows sunken, dimpled, corky distortions, the puckered catfaced look, where feeding occurred on young fruit. The damage is cosmetic on the surface but can run into the flesh; it does not spread or rot on its own.

beginner: A handful of insects, chiefly stink bugs and the small tarnished plant bug, that poke the young apricots to feed. The spot they feed on stops growing while the rest of the fruit swells around it, leaving a dimple. Because apricots set fruit early, the little fruit is out just as these bugs get going in spring.
seasoned: Several true bugs, mainly stink bugs and the tarnished plant bug, that puncture small apricots to feed. Tissue at each feeding point stops growing while the surrounding flesh keeps swelling, so the mature fruit is left puckered and corky. Apricot ripens early, so the vulnerable young-fruit stage overlaps the spring buildup of these bugs.

beginner: Spraying a single tree does not help much, because these bugs come in from weeds and brush nearby. The better fix is to take away their hiding spots: mow and pull the broadleaf weeds around the tree, especially in spring while the fruit is small.
seasoned: Spraying one tree does little, since these bugs commute in from nearby weeds and brush. The practical control is to deny them that harborage: mow and clear the broadleaf weeds around the tree, especially through spring when young fruit is most vulnerable.

beginner: Keep the ground around the tree mowed and clear of broadleaf weeds, which is where these bugs live and breed. A clean, grassy area around the tree means fewer of them ever reach your apricots.
seasoned: Keep the surrounding ground mowed and free of the broadleaf weeds these bugs breed in; a clean, grassy strip around the tree is the single biggest thing that lowers how many reach the fruit.

beginner: At bloom, flowers go limp and brown and small gummy dead patches form on the nearby spurs. As apricots ripen, brown spots appear and spread quickly, sometimes rotting a whole fruit in a day or two in warm, wet weather, with a dusty tan fuzz on top. Rotted fruit shrivels into a hard mummy that hangs on. Apricot catches brown rot more easily than almost any other fruit.
seasoned: At bloom, infected blossoms wilt and brown and the infection runs into the spur to form a small gummy canker. As fruit ripens, firm brown spots appear and spread fast, rotting a whole apricot within a day or two in warm, wet weather, with a dusty tan spore mass on the surface. Rotted fruit dries into a clinging mummy. Apricot is among the most brown-rot-susceptible of all stone fruit.

beginner: A fungus called Monilinia. It survives winter in dried mummy fruit and dead twig patches, then releases spores at bloom that infect the flowers, which later cause the fruit to rot. Warm, wet weather makes it spread fast, which is why apricots do much better in dry-summer climates than in humid ones.
seasoned: The fungus Monilinia (M. fructicola and M. laxa). It overwinters in mummies and twig cankers; spores at bloom infect flowers, and those infections later seed the fruit rot. Warm, humid, wet weather drives it, which is a large part of why apricot is a poor risk in the humid Southeast and better in dry western summers.

beginner: Cleanup is the main control: take off and destroy every dried mummy from the tree and ground and prune out the gummy dead twig patches, which hold the spores. If bloom is wet, an organic-approved spray at bloom helps protect the flowers. Pick on time, handle gently, and throw out any rotting fruit right away.
seasoned: Sanitation is the core control: remove and destroy every mummy from the tree and ground and prune out gummy twig cankers, since these are the spore sources. In a wet bloom, an organic-approved bloom-time fungicide reduces blossom blight. Pick promptly, handle gently, and remove any rotting fruit at once; an open, fast-drying canopy is a standing defense.

beginner: Cleaning up all year prevents most of it: never leave dried mummies over winter, prune so the tree is open and dries fast after rain, and pick on time. In wet climates you will likely need an organic-approved spray at bloom and again near harvest, because apricot is so prone to this disease.
seasoned: Year-round sanitation prevents most loss: never leave mummies over winter, keep the canopy open with pruning so fruit dries fast after rain, harvest promptly, and favor a dry-summer site. In humid regions, plan on a bloom and pre-harvest fungicide program, since apricot's high susceptibility makes sanitation alone insufficient.

beginner: Sunken, dark, gummy patches (cankers) on the trunk and branches that ooze amber sap, often killing the branch above them. In spring, flowers and buds may blacken and die, and some buds never open. It is one of the worst apricot diseases and hits harder on trees grown on plum rootstocks.
seasoned: Sunken, dark, gummy cankers on trunk, scaffolds, and spurs that ooze amber gum, often girdling and killing limbs; in spring, blossoms and spurs blast (blacken and die) and dormant buds fail to open. It is one of the most serious apricot diseases and is worse on trees grown on plum rootstocks (Myrobalan, Marianna), which are especially susceptible.

beginner: A bacterium (a microscopic organism) called Pseudomonas syringae. It gets in through wounds, leaf scars, and frost damage during cool, wet weather, and is worse on stressed trees, those in wet soil, hit by frost, or pushed with too much nitrogen. Apricot blooms so early that its tender new growth often meets the cold, wet weather this disease loves.
seasoned: The bacterium Pseudomonas syringae. It infects through wounds, leaf scars, and frost-injured tissue in cool, wet spring and fall weather, and is worsened by anything that stresses the tree: poor drainage, ring nematodes, frost, and high-nitrogen soft growth. Apricot's very early bloom exposes fresh tissue to exactly the cold, wet spells that favor it.

beginner: There is no cure once it sets in. The approach is prevention: cut out the cankered wood well below the dead patch during dry summer weather (not in wet spring), clean your tools between cuts, and pull out a badly infected young tree. Keep the tree healthy, unstressed, and on well-drained ground; copper sprays only help a little.
seasoned: There is no cure once a tree is infected. Management is preventive: cut out cankered wood well below the canker in dry summer weather (not in wet spring), disinfecting tools between cuts, and remove badly infected young trees. Keep the tree unstressed and well drained; copper sprays give only partial protection and resistance is common.

beginner: Prevention is everything: plant where the soil drains well, pick a more resistant rootstock (a peach seedling like Lovell resists it better than plum rootstocks), avoid frosty low spots and trunk wounds, paint the trunk white to prevent sunburn cracks, prune only in dry summer weather, and do not over-feed. A healthy, unstressed tree on good ground shrugs it off best.
seasoned: Prevention is everything: plant on well-drained ground, choose a tolerant rootstock (a peach seedling such as Lovell is more canker-tolerant than the plum stocks), avoid frost-pocket sites and trunk wounds, paint the trunk white against sunscald cracks, prune only in dry summer weather, and never push soft growth with late nitrogen.

beginner: Leaves get small angular water-soaked spots that turn brown and fall out, leaving little holes, called a shot-hole look. Bad cases turn leaves yellow and thin out the tree. On the fruit, small sunken spots and skin cracks form. How badly a tree is hit depends a lot on the variety and on how humid your area is.
seasoned: Small angular, water-soaked spots on leaves turn brown and drop out, leaving a shot-hole look; heavy infection yellows and thins the canopy. On fruit, small sunken spots and cracks develop on the skin. Susceptibility varies by cultivar, and pressure is highest in warm, humid regions.

beginner: A bacterium (a microscopic organism, not a fungus) called Xanthomonas. It spreads in warm, wet weather and builds up when there are other susceptible stone-fruit trees close by. Its leaf holes can look like the fungal shot hole disease, which is a different problem.
seasoned: The bacterium Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni. It spreads in warm, wet weather and builds up where susceptible stone fruit grow nearby. On apricot the leaf and fruit spotting is sometimes confused with the fungal shot hole (Coryneum blight).

beginner: There is no good home cure once it shows up. Copper sprays help a little as prevention but can hurt the tree if overused, so they are not a dependable fix. The best you can do is keep the tree healthy and open so the leaves dry fast.
seasoned: Home options are limited once symptoms appear: copper sprays help more as prevention than cure and can injure the tree if overused, so they are not a reliable home fix. Keeping the tree vigorous and the canopy open and dry helps it tolerate the disease.

beginner: The best prevention is the variety and the site you pick. A tolerant variety on a spot with dry summers and good airflow avoids most of the trouble, so it is a decision to make before planting. A healthy, open tree also helps.
seasoned: The most effective measure is choosing a resistant or tolerant cultivar and a dry-summer site; this is largely a decision made before the tree goes in. Good airflow, an open canopy, and tree vigor reduce severity.

beginner: Small reddish-purple spots on the leaves whose brown centers fall out, leaving neat round holes that look like the leaf was hit with birdshot. It also spots the fruit and can kill buds. A bad case drops a lot of leaves and weakens the tree. Apricot is one of its favorite hosts.
seasoned: Small reddish-purple spots on leaves whose centers turn brown, die, and drop out, leaving clean round holes as if shot with birdshot. It also spots the fruit and can kill dormant buds and cause small twig cankers with gumming. Heavy infection defoliates and weakens the tree; apricot is a classic host.

beginner: A fungus (Coryneum blight) that spends winter in infected buds and twigs and spreads in cool, wet spring weather and wherever water splashes the leaves. Overhead sprinklers that wet the tree make it much worse.
seasoned: The fungus Wilsonomyces carpophilus (Coryneum blight). It overwinters in infected buds and twig lesions and spreads in cool, wet spring weather and by splashing water and overhead irrigation. Wet springs and sprinkler wetting of the canopy drive it.

beginner: Cut out infected twigs, rake up and destroy fallen spotted leaves, and water at the ground rather than over the top so the leaves stay dry. A copper spray on the bare, dormant tree in late winter is the main way to protect it where this disease is common.
seasoned: Prune out infected twigs and buds, rake and destroy fallen infected leaves, and switch irrigation to the root zone so the canopy stays dry. A dormant application of fixed copper on the leafless tree is the main protective spray where the disease is established.

beginner: The biggest thing is keeping the leaves dry: water at the ground, not over the tree, prune so air moves through, and clean up fallen leaves. In wet-spring areas, a copper spray on the bare tree in late winter protects it.
seasoned: Keep water off the canopy (drip or soaker, never overhead), prune for airflow, clear fallen leaves, and apply a dormant copper spray in wet-spring regions. Dry-summer irrigation discipline is the single biggest lever.

beginner: Water deeply now and then instead of a little every day. Plan on about once or twice a week while a young tree is getting established, easing to about once a week for a fruiting tree in summer heat, adjusting for rain and your soil. Apricot hates soggy soil, so let the surface dry out between waterings. In winter, when the tree is resting, it needs very little and rain usually covers it.
seasoned: Water deep-and-infrequent rather than little-and-often: about once or twice a week while a young tree establishes, easing to roughly weekly (a deep soak) for a bearing tree in summer heat, always adjusted for rain and soil. Apricot resents constantly wet soil, so let the top of the root zone dry between soaks. Through winter dormancy water need drops sharply and rainfall usually suffices.

beginner: Each time you water, give a deep soak that reaches all the way down to the roots, not just a splash on top. A young tree wants about 3 to 5 gallons per soak. An older, fruiting tree wants roughly an inch of water a week through the season, and more when it is hot, given as deep soaks. Steady water while the fruit is filling out makes bigger apricots.
seasoned: Water deeply each time so moisture reaches the full root zone, not just the surface. For an establishing tree, on the order of 3 to 5 gallons per soak; for a bearing tree, roughly the equivalent of an inch of water per week through the season, more in heat, delivered as deep soaks to a 3-foot depth. Steady moisture through the final swell sizes the fruit.

beginner: Water at the ground around the roots with a drip line or soaker hose, and keep the leaves and fruit dry. Spraying water over the top wets the leaves and helps diseases like brown rot and shot hole, so put the water on the soil, not the tree. Spread it across the root area out to the edge of the branches, not just right at the trunk.
seasoned: Water at the root zone by drip or soaker and keep the canopy and fruit dry. Overhead watering that wets the leaves feeds brown rot, shot hole, and bacterial canker, so deliver water to the soil, not the tree. Apply it across the root area out toward the drip line rather than only at the trunk.

beginner: Too much water, or soil that drains poorly, shows up as yellowing leaves, wilting that does not go away even when the soil is wet, and a tree that slowly goes downhill, because the roots cannot breathe. In apricot, soil that stays wet also brings on crown and root rot and the serious disease bacterial canker. Soil that never dries out between waterings is your warning to back off.
seasoned: Overwatering and poor drainage show as yellowing leaves, wilting that persists even in wet soil, and a declining tree, since apricot roots suffocate in soggy ground. Chronically wet soil also brings on crown and root rot and predisposes the trunk to bacterial canker, both often fatal. Soil that never dries between waterings is the warning sign to act on.

beginner: Too little water shows as wilting, dull curling leaves, slower growth, and leaves dropping early in a long dry spell. The clearest sign is in the fruit: a tree that runs short of water while the apricots are sizing up makes small, less sweet fruit, even though the tree itself lives through it. Try to catch the dry stress before the fruit suffers for it.
seasoned: Underwatering shows as wilting, dull curling leaves, slowed shoot growth, and early leaf drop in a long dry spell. The most telling symptom is on the fruit: a tree short of water during the final swell sizes its apricots poorly, leaving them small and less sweet even though the tree survives. Catch the dry stress before the fruit pays for it.

beginner: While the tree is getting established, keep the soil around the roots evenly moist but not soggy. A deep soak of about 3 to 5 gallons once or twice a week, more in heat and less after rain, helps the tree grow the deep roots it needs.
seasoned: Through establishment, keep the root ball and surrounding soil consistently moist, never waterlogged. Deep soaks of about 3 to 5 gallons once or twice a week, adjusted for rain and heat, build the deep root system the tree relies on later.

beginner: While the apricots are sizing up and coloring, keep the water steady. Aim for about an inch of water a week as deep soaks. Steady watering now is what gives you bigger, sweeter fruit.
seasoned: As the fruit sizes and colors, keep moisture steady. Aim for about an inch of water per week as deep soaks and avoid a dry-then-wet swing. Consistent soil moisture through this window is what sizes and sweetens the crop.

beginner: After the leaves drop and the tree is resting for winter, it needs very little water. Let rain do most of the work and only water during long dry stretches so the roots do not dry out. Do not keep the soil soaked in winter.
seasoned: Once dormant and leafless, water need drops sharply; rely on rainfall and water only in prolonged dry spells so roots do not desiccate. Avoid keeping dormant soil saturated, which invites root rot and canker.

beginner: Give the tree a deep soak now and then rather than a little every day, and water at the ground (a drip line or soaker hose is ideal) instead of spraying the leaves, since wet leaves lead to disease. Young trees need steady moisture for their first couple of years. Older trees handle some dry spells, but the apricots come out small if the tree gets too dry, and the roots rot if it stays too wet.
seasoned: Water deeply and infrequently at the root zone, by drip or soaker, to drive deep rooting; never wet the canopy, which feeds brown rot, shot hole, and bacterial canker. Young trees need consistent moisture through their first two seasons to establish; mature apricots are moderately drought-tolerant but size fruit poorly under stress and resent standing water.

render_evidence: no renderer; watering is in herb FACT_KEYS

beginner: The most important time to keep the tree watered is the last 2 to 3 weeks before harvest, when the apricots do most of their growing. If the tree runs dry then, the fruit stays small and watering later will not fix it. The few weeks right after bloom matter too. seasoned: The make-or-break window is the final swell, roughly the last 2 to 3 weeks before harvest, when cell expansion adds most of the fruit's final size. seasoned: Apricot is a deciduous stone-fruit tree (Prunus armeniaca) prized for fruit that ripens best tree-ripened at home, where it can hang to full flavor rather than being picked firm for shipping. It is self-fruitful, so a single tree bears, and it ripens earlier than peach. Its defining trait, and its defining challenge, is that it blooms earlier than almost any other fruit tree: the open flowers meet late frosts most springs on a frost-prone site, so variety choice and a frost-aware location matter more than anything. It also asks for real work: an annual dormant pruning to an open center, disease management (brown rot above all, plus bacterial canker and shot hole), early fruit thinning, and enough winter chill to break dormancy. Given a dry-summer or frost-safe site and that care, a backyard apricot rewards you with fruit grocery shelves cannot match.

The most dependable apricot regions are dry-summer areas with cold-enough winters to hold bloom back and dependable, frost-free springs (interior California and the Intermountain West are classic). The warm edge (zones 9 and warmer) is limited by too little winter chill and, in the humid Southeast, by heavy disease. Match a late-blooming, cold-hardy cultivar to a frost-safe site and you give yourself the best odds.

beginner: Apricot trees need enough cold winter hours, called chill hours, before they will bloom properly in spring. Most kinds want about 600 to 900 hours, and a few low-chill types like Katy need only about 350. Apricot needs less winter cold than most fruit trees, which is part of why it blooms so early. In mild-winter areas, choose a low-chill variety so it blooms evenly; in cold areas, a higher-chill, late-blooming variety both fits your winters and helps the tree bloom later, after the worst frosts have passed.
seasoned: Apricots need a stretch of winter cold, counted as chill hours (hours between 32°F and 45°F), to break dormancy and bloom evenly. Most cultivars want about 600 to 900 hours, with a few low-chill types (Katy) bearing on roughly 350. Apricot's chill requirement is on the low side for a stone fruit, which is exactly why it satisfies its chill and blooms so early, and why late frost, not chill, is usually the crop-limiting factor. In mild-winter regions choose a low-chill cultivar so bloom is at least even; in cold regions a higher-chill, late-blooming cultivar both fits the chill and delays bloom past the worst frosts.

beginner: Most apricots are self-fruitful, which means one tree makes fruit by itself with no second tree needed. This is different from many cherries and apples, which do need a partner. A few kinds, mainly Moorpark, make a fuller crop when a second apricot blooms nearby, but even they fruit on their own, so a partner is a bonus and not a must. Bees do the pollinating, so anything that helps bees be active during the short, early bloom helps the tree set fruit, even a single tree.
seasoned: Most apricots are self-fruitful, so a single tree sets a full crop on its own without a pollinizer; this is the inverse of many sweet cherries and apples, which require cross-pollination. A few cultivars, chiefly Moorpark, set a heavier crop with a compatible second variety blooming at the same time, but even they fruit alone, so a pollinizer is an optional bonus rather than a requirement. Apricots are insect-pollinated, mainly by bees, so supporting pollinator activity during the short, very early bloom helps set even on a lone tree, especially in cool springs.

beginner: The first year is about helping the tree settle in, not getting fruit. Pull off any fruit that forms. Wait to fertilize until the tree starts growing, and never feed late in the year.
seasoned: In the planting year, prioritize establishment over fruit. Remove any fruit that sets. Hold fertilizer until growth begins, and never feed late in the season.
